extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal historians, and practitioners studying English common law (Crown revenue, property escheat, guardianship of idiots/lunatics, and taxation)
extracted.subtask_short: English common law: revenue and guardianship
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of rules and doctrines governing the king's ordinary and extraordinary revenue (deodands, escheats, customs, excise, land/malt taxes, subsidies) and the legal status/guardianship of idiots and lunatics under English common law and statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deodand presentation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A thing is not a deodand unless it is presented as such by a jury of twelve men; the instrument of death and the value must be presented and found by the grand jury (e.g., stroke given with a certain penknife, value sixpence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No deodands are due unless presented by a jury; presentation of instrument and valuation by jury is essential. (Examples and footnotes cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Deodands and maritime exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: No deodands are due for accidents happening upon the high sea, as being out of the jurisdiction of the common law; but if a man falls from a boat or ship in fresh water and is drowned, the vessel and cargo are in strictness a deodand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictional rule: deodand liability depends on forum (high sea excluded; fresh water within jurisdiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal grantability of forfeitures and incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Deodands, forfeitures, wrecks, treasure trove, royal fish, mines, waifs, and estrays may be granted by the king to particular subjects as a royal franchise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such franchises were commonly granted to lords of manors or other liberties, often diverting original public design to private benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escheat rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Lands revert to and vest in the king upon defect of heirs to succeed to the inheritance; the king is, in the eye of the law, the original proprietor of all lands in the kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone notes fuller discussion of how lands may be acquired or lost by escheat is in the second book; principle establishes escheat as a branch of the king's ordinary revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'idiot' (natural fool)
rubrics_metrics.description: An idiot, or natural fool, is one that hath had no understanding from his nativity; by law presumed never likely to attain any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this presumption, custody of the person and lands was vested in the lord of the fee historically and later in the king to prevent waste; some manor customs may differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory wardship of natural fools (17 Edw. II. c. 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute directs that the king shall have ward of the lands of natural fools, taking the profits without waste or destruction, and shall find them necessaries; after their death the king shall render the estate to the heirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: prevent idiots from aliening lands and heirs from being disinherited; affirms common law; fiscal prerogative described as part of king's ordinary revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writ de idiota inquirendo and jury trial
rubrics_metrics.description: By the old common law there is a writ de idiota inquirendo to enquire whether a man be an idiot or not, which must be tried by a jury of twelve men; if they find him purus idiota, the profits of his lands and the custody of his person may be granted by the king to some subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding of nativity-based idiocy (purus idiota) has distinct legal consequences (royal wardship/benefit); such grants have been viewed as a hardship and were occasionally revisited by Parliament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is not an idiot (practical test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is not an idiot if he hath any glimmering of reason, so that he can tell his parents, his age, or the like common matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative practical threshold: minimal communicative/recognitional abilities rebut 'idiot' status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons born deaf, dumb, and blind treated as idiots
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who is born deaf, dumb, and blind is looked upon by the law as in the same state with an idiot, being supposed incapable of understanding, as wanting those senses which furnish the human mind with ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Birth-caused sensory deprivation is treated as legal idiocy for purposes of custody and wardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'lunatic' / non compos mentis
rubrics_metrics.description: A lunatic, or non compos mentis, is one who hath had understanding, but by disease, grief, or other accident hath lost the use of his reason; lunatic implies lucid intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The category non compos mentis includes lunatics, persons under frenzies, those who lose intellect by disease, or who grow deaf/dumb/blind (not born so), i.e., anyone rendered incapable of conducting their own affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory care for lunatics (17 Edw. II. c. 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute declares that the king shall provide for the custody and sustentation of lunatics, and preserve their lands and the profits of them for their use when they come to their right mind; the king shall take nothing to his own use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King acts as trustee for lunatics; if they recover, accounting required; if they die, residue distribution follows ordinary's advice and later administration law to executors/administrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for proving non compos mentis
rubrics_metrics.description: The lord chancellor, by special authority from the king, grants a commission in nature of the writ de idiota inquirendo to enquire into the party's state of mind; if found non compos, the care of his person with suitable allowance is usually committed to a friend called his committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent abuse, the next heir is never permitted to be committee of the person (conflict of interest); the heir is often made manager/committee of the estate but is accountable to the court of chancery and to the non compos if he recovers, or to administrators if not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule disqualifying heir as committee of person
rubrics_metrics.description: The next heir is never permitted to be the committee of the person of a lunatic/idiot, because it is his interest that the party should die.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court preference: avoid conflicts by appointing a friend for personal custody; next of kin (if not heir) may serve since interest differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman law approach to prodigality versus English rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Roman law a man notorious for prodigality might be looked upon as non compos and committed to curators/tutors; under English law, if an inquest returns a man an 'unthrift' and not an 'idiot', no further proceedings follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative note: Blackstone questions propriety of Roman approach and defends English liberty to use property, limited by 'sic utere tuo, ut alienum non laedas'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary revenue: grants by commons (aids/subsidies/supplies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary grants called aids, subsidies, and supplies are granted by the commons in parliament, who when they have voted a supply usually resolve into a committee of ways and means to consider ways and means of raising it; the committee's resolutions, when approved by the house, are generally final and conclusive though an act of the whole parliament is required to raise the supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any member may propose taxation schemes; money is often advanced on credit of a vote of the house before a law is passed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: taxes require parliamentary assent
rubrics_metrics.description: The king shall not take any aids, tasks, talliage or tax without the common assent of the great men and commons in parliament (historic statutes and Magna Carta clauses cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional limit on royal taxation; historical statutes (Edward I, Magna Carta, subsequent acts) established parliamentary consent as prerequisite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual taxes: land tax and malt tax (definitions and history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual taxes commonly are those upon land and malt. The land tax in modern shape superseded tenths, fifteenths, scutages, hydages, and talliages; malt tax is a duty (since 1697) of 6d per bushel on malt and proportionable sums on certain liquors, under excise commissioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone provides historical origin and mechanics: tenths/fifteenths were on movables; scutage arose from military tenure; land tax assessed by county commissions based on 1692 valuation; malt tax handled by excise and further permanent excise additions noted (1760, 1763).

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs duties: origin, types, and policy considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs are duties payable upon merchandise exported and imported; historically justified because the king permitted departure and maintained ports. Ancient hereditary customs (e.g., on wool, skins, leather) and later distinctions (prisage/butlerage, subsidies, tonnage, poundage) are described; aliens paid larger proportions (alien's duty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customs are paid by merchants and ultimately by consumers; heavy imposts can check trade and encourage smuggling, which in turn undermines ordinary confiscation penalties and may demand extraordinary punishments; timing of taxation in the supply chain affects burden on consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and consequences of excise duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The excise is an inland imposition, paid sometimes upon consumption or retail sale; it is the most economical way of taxing (lower levying/collection costs) but requires stringent enforcement powers (entry and search of houses) and summary proceedings that can exclude jury trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of arbitrary and summary enforcement, excises were unpopular and politically sensitive; historically introduced 1643, initially on beer/ale/cider/perry, later expanded to many commodities; 'use the people to it by little and little' rationale noted.
